The Election of 1876. The most disputed result in American history until two thousand occurred in this election between Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel Tilden. Tilden won the popular vote by a decisive margin and held the edge in electoral votes, but disputed returns from the three remaining reconstructed southern states threw the outcome into chaos. A specially created Electoral Commission, controlled by Republicans, awarded all contested electors to Hayes in exchange for the Compromise of eighteen seventy-seven—which ended Reconstruction and abandoned freed slaves to southern white rule.

Samuel Tilden won the popular vote with fifty-one percent and carried one hundred eighty-four electoral votes, needing only one more for victory. Rutherford Hayes held one hundred sixty-five electoral votes; twenty electors from South Carolina, Florida, and Louisiana were disputed. Each state sent conflicting returns: Republican canvassing boards submitted one set; Democratic authorities submitted another—fraud and intimidation likely on both sides.

Congress created a fifteen-member Electoral Commission with eight Republicans and seven Democrats to adjudicate the disputes. The Commission voted eight-to-seven on every disputed return, always for Hayes, awarding him the presidency by one electoral vote—one hundred eighty-five to one hundred eighty-four. The backroom deal: Hayes would end federal protection for freed slaves in the South, withdraw the last occupation troops, and allow southern whites to regain political control.

Hayes became president despite losing the popular vote—a setback for democratic legitimacy. Reconstruction ended; the Solid South emerged as a Democratic stronghold, solidifying white southern power for nearly a century. The 1876 election represents the moment when the promise of Reconstruction—equality before law for all Americans—was sacrificed to sectional reunion.
